GYXY: Suppose incomes take finitely many values. An income distribution records what share of the population earns each value, so formally it looks just like a lottery.
9E1M: Based on Miyamoto, Wakker, Bleichrodt and Peters (1998). An agent weighs length of life against its quality.
N9PG: An agent always computes 2+3 as 6. Build a money-pump argument that exploits him, and assess how convincing it is.
RPWH: Fix a finite set A of activities. A schedule for a day is a finite sequence such as: activity a1​ between 0 and t1​, activity a2​ between t1​ and t1​+t2​, and so forth.
K7S8: This problem follows Rothschild and Stiglitz (1970).
1C8Z: This problem follows Slovic and Lichtenstein (1968).
ASDQ: Consider a consumer who ranks K-tuples giving the amounts held of K risky assets.
PSHT: This problem follows Rubinstein (2002). Adam’s only food in the Garden of Eden is apples.
CXGA: This problem follows Yaari (1987). Expected utility has the form U(p)=∑k=1K​Gp​(zk​)[u(zk​)−u(zk−1​)], with z0​<z1​<⋯<zK​ the support prizes of p and Gp​(zk​)=∑j≥k​p(zj​). Define W(p)=∑k=1K​f(Gp​(zk​))[zk​−zk−1​], for a continuous, increasing f:[0,1]→[0,1].
540E: Draw a number 2n with probability 2n/3n+1, then place 2n in one envelope and 2n+1 in another. You get one envelope at random; your friend gets the other.
1S2E: There are two actions, x and y. Each pays a sure money prize once the state of nature is fixed; the state is A with probability α and B with probability 1−α. The agent is an expected-utility maximizer.
44KZ: Suppose there are two or more individuals and three or more alternatives. Show that IIA fails for every Borda rule.
C9V6: This problem follows May (1952). Society faces just two alternatives in X.
YVPG: Take X=[0,1] and suppose each person’s preference is single-peaked: person i has some alternative ai∗​ with b≻i​c in case ai∗​≥b>c or c>b≥ai∗​. Restrict the domain to such preferences.
KV0P: Each member of a society N picks one element of a set X, read as the social action that member proposes.
3TEW: Decisive and almost decisive coalitions appear in several proofs of Arrow’s theorem. Fix an SWF.
DQ5W: This problem follows Kasher and Rubinstein (1997). Who counts as an economist? View this as pooling the opinions of a department’s members.
XF6A: Let ≿ be a complete, reflexive and transitive preference relation on a set X, and define x∼y⟺(x≿y)∧(y≿x) and x≻y⟺(x≿y)∧¬(y≿x). Prove:
NEFW: (MWG Exercise 1.B.3.) Show that if f:R→R is strictly increasing and u:X→R is a utility function representing the preference relation ≿, then v=f∘u, v(x)=f(u(x)), is also a utility function representing ≿.
KFSX: With X finite, every complete, reflexive and transitive preference has a utility representation.
WPRG: A study surveys 2034 Australians to place a dollar value on preserving the Kakadu Conservation Zone and finds benefits far exceeding costs.
3Y6Y: A consumer satisfies the von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms and is strictly risk averse.
185R: Citizens share a von Neumann–Morgenstern utility u(w) that is as smooth as needed, strictly increasing and concave.
ZSF9: (Adapted from MWG Exercise 6.B.5.) Work with lotteries over three outcomes.
AD12: Standard financial advice holds that younger people should invest a higher fraction of their wealth in stocks than older people. Discuss why this might, or might not, make sense.
S9ZZ: (Adapted from MWG Exercise 3.D.5, parts (a), (c) and (d).) With two goods, take the CES utility function u(x)=(x1ρ​+x2ρ​)1/ρ (MWG Exercise 3.C.6’s function with α1​=α2​=1).
WPSR: (Adapted from MWG Exercise 3.G.6, parts (a), (b) and (c).) There are three goods, priced p1​,p2​,p3​. A consumer with wealth w>0 demands the first two goods according to x1​x2​​=100−5p3​p1​​+βp3​p2​​+δp3​w​,=α+βp3​p1​​+γp3​p2​​+δp3​w​,​ in which α, β, γ and δ are constants, none of them zero.
EQWH: Let the consumption set be (−∞,∞)×R+n−1​, and suppose that preferences are strictly convex and quasi-linear in the first good. Normalize p1​=1.
EN4K: A consumer of two goods has utility function u(x,y)=max{ax,ay}+min{x,y}, with 0<a<1.
85D0: Over five years, the price of single-family homes in the Boston area rose dramatically, while the rents charged for single-family homes offered for rent rose only a little.
ETHS: A consumer has a continuous, strictly increasing, quasi-concave utility function, and the consumer’s expenditure function is known to be e(p1​,p2​,u)=p1​+p2​p1​p2​​u.
ZTWY: (Adapted from MWG Exercise 4.D.5.) An economy has I consumers.
B245: (Adapted from MWG Exercise 3.I.2.) A consumer has wealth w>0 and initially faces prices p0. A per-unit tax t on good 1 lifts that good’s price to p10​+t; call the new price vector p1. The tax collects T=tx1​(p1,w). Write u0=v(p0,w) and u1=v(p1,w), let h1​(p1​,u) denote Hicksian demand for good 1 with the other prices held fixed, and let pˉ​1​=p10​+t be the after-tax price.
ZFCH: Goods i and j are said to be substitutes at (p,u) if ∂hi​(p,u)/∂pj​≥0.
4C7H: Consider a consumer with indirect utility function v(p1​,p2​,I)=I/p1​p2​​.
NQ92: Consider a monopolist with cost function c(q)=cq. Use a simple revealed preference argument to show that the monopolist’s output is weakly decreasing in c. (One can do this very generally, without making any assumptions about the demand curve.)
DYEK: Let Q(p,θ) be a downward-sloping demand curve, let θ be a parameter of the demand curve, and suppose that Q is differentiable in p and strictly positive in the relevant region of prices.
C2MD: Suppose there are two inputs to production, technology and the skill level of a single worker who uses the technology.
JRZ3: Two states can occur, s=1,2. Two securities trade: a stock priced at 1 and a bond priced at B≥0. In state s the stock returns Rs​; the bond returns r>0 in both states.
B2RW: At the start, player 1 picks a, b or c. Choosing a stops play with payoffs (1,0,0). Following b, player 2 picks d or e. Following c, player 2 picks f or g; the move g stops play with payoffs (2,2,0). The histories bd, be and cf all lead to player 3, who does not know which of them occurred and picks h or i. Payoffs from h and from i, in that order, are: (3,0,2) and (0,2,1) following bd; (0,1,1) and (4,1,2) following be; (1,1,1) and (0,3,2) following cf.
C249: A company employs two salespeople, r and e. Sales of agent i are xi​=ai​+εi​, with ai​ the effort chosen and εr​,εe​ independent draws from one density g. Neither agent cares about risk, and both dislike effort.
A4FG: Let X be a set and Λ a set of primitive orderings on X. A preference relation ≿ on X, complete and transitive, is Λ-convex if for all a,b∈X.
R0PH: Let X be a convex and closed subset of RN. Each nonzero vector v defines the algebraic linear ordering x≥v​y if v⋅x≥v⋅y; let Ψ be the set of all of them.
CTK2: Let X be a set, ≿ a preference relation on X and Λ a set of orderings on X; for ⊵∈Λ write ▹ for its strict part.
